$schema_note: Per-app rule WEIGHTINGS, and nothing else. One review harness, three problems.
🚨 This file holds POLICY ONLY. It carries no fact about any app's stack --
no framework, no version, no CSS engine, no token map. PIPELINE_SPEC C11 is a
table that banned prose as a source and then published three unmeasured cells
of its own; the ruling was that stack facts must be GENERATED into
profiles.json by reading the checkouts, never written down. So the two kinds
of profile are kept apart: that generated artifact says what an app IS, this
one says what we CARE about, and only the second is a judgement a person makes.
Availability is expressed as a REQUIREMENT, never as a claim. A profile that
needs a token map to score conformance says so in `requires`; the router then
reports those classes UNVERIFIED whenever the run does not supply one. An app
whose class names are runtime hashes therefore abstains because the token map
is absent at run time -- not because this file asserted something about it. A
silent zero on a rule that could not run is the failure this shape prevents.

routing.$note: Which rule classes are questions rather than verdicts, and what closes them. The T1 subtraction reads this; it is code, not discipline (C16).

contrast-indeterminate.asks: what is the contrast where the text actually sits

unscreenable_classes.$note: T2. Never derived from a finding, never cut for budget -- these are the questions no rule can ask, so their absence from the deterministic pass means nothing at all.
unscreenable_classes.hierarchy: does the eye land on the action the page wants first
unscreenable_classes.gestalt: do the groupings the layout implies match the ones the content has
unscreenable_classes.content-fit: does the copy fit the space it was given, at this length
unscreenable_classes.semantic-coherence: does what the page says match what it shows
unscreenable_classes.optical-alignment: does anything read as misaligned that measures as aligned
unscreenable_classes.readability: can this be read at a glance, at the size it ships

never_ask_a_model: any distance, gap, size, ratio or contrast value -- solid or gradient

corpus.emphasis: everything, unweighted -- the bench measures rules, not products
corpus.why: A profile that demoted anything would make the false-positive budget a measurement of the profile rather than of the rule.

why: A purchased template carries its own internal design system, coherent and
not ours. Scoring it against our tokens produces a page of true statements
that are not defects -- the ~20% false-positive cliff reached by being
right about the wrong question. What a landing page fails at is the part
no rule can ask: whether the eye lands where the page wanted it.
So conformance is demoted, correctness is not demoted at all (a contrast
failure is a failure whoever authored the CSS), and the crop budget is
spent on the unscreenable classes.
An app we author against tokens we own is the one case where the
deterministic layer does nearly all the work: every conformance question
has a number in the answer, so none of it belongs to a model. Drift here
is a real defect rather than a difference of authorship, and it compounds
-- one off-scale size becomes the precedent for the next.
The vision queue is correspondingly small: it exists for the six
unscreenable classes and for whatever the deterministic pass could not
resolve, and for nothing else.

reso-web-app.emphasis: between the two -- and it must say which half it could not check
why: Conformance rules need a token map to mean anything: without one,
'no drift found' is not a pass, it is a rule that never ran. This profile
therefore REQUIRES a token map and lets the router mark those classes
UNVERIFIED when the run cannot supply one, which is the honest report and
the same shape as rule 6's third answer.
